posts.body:
It's been a while! I've been preparing for my Nepal trip, going camping for the first time (aside: who knew that Jervis Bay is a part of it's own territory and not in NSW!?) and Ozark binging with Leesa. During that time, I've done 3 more AoPS problems (we're at 385) and the latest problem showed my weaknesses with reasoning and manipulating proportions. So that was the springboard into me doing some outside problems in proportions.

More interesting than the problems themselves, is the SRS app / study planner that acts as the "pen and paper" that my Codex sessions can look at to tailor my learning and set me homework challenges after our socratic tutoring sessions. It's called commonplace which I feel is a sick name, as it's true! I want the knowledge that I found difficult today, to be commonplace in a near future. It's all hosted in Codex sites backed by (free) Cloudflare D1, but it started out as a localhost app. However, with the Nepal trip coming up soon and me not wanting to bring my laptop, I didn't want to miss any days which means accessible via the phone. I do feel a bit weird with vendor lock with Codex hosting the website, but just as easy as I made the app, I can also migrate it anywhere else with a single prompt. Crazy times.

Anyhoo onto the math! I scrapped my math supervision skill, in favour for Jane Street's [socratic tutor skill](https://github.com/janestreet/agent_skills/blob/master/socratic-tutor/SKILL.md) but I still find that it's not that much of an upgrade. I really like that it scopes out a syllabus and evaluates your skills against that syllabus to figure out what it needs to teach me, but it still suffers from that "no thread story that motivates all the learning" and quickly will jump into examples without motivating questions being asked.

A cool problem that reminded me of the simple harmonic motion days in high school was: 
> Assume the period $T$ depends only on pendulum length $L$ and gravitational acceleration $g$. Use dimensions to derive the dependence on $L$ and $g$ up to a numerical constant. Then read Example 2.3.1 in [MIT OpenCourseWare’s Dimensional Analysis](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-01sc-classical-mechanics-fall-2016/mit8_01scs22_chapter2.pdf) and write what changes when the starting angle is included.

Dimensional analysis is always something I've used when trying to figure out weird ratios in my head (like omg when I try to convert running pace $\mathrm{min}/\mathrm{km}$ to $\mathrm{km}/\mathrm{h}$ and try to fandangle the units to make sense as if they were programming types). This was nice to see it in it's OG use case which is in physical problems! I often use dimensional analysis to convert ratios, but the table in the MIT handout where they enumerated all the variables that could influence the period showed that it's really useful in guesstimating what equations could look like. For example, the mass of the pendulum was one of the variables, but because none of the other brainstormed variables had mass as a unit, it was assumed that it wasn't consequential and discarded. Of course, this could be incorrect in other cases, but it's a technique that can help one form hypothesis quickly, and then use experimentation / intuition to test it. 

The release angle and how it affects period is something that I'm still trying to figure out. It looks like it's $2\pi$ when the release angle is sufficiently small, but I'm yet to grok how we got $2\pi$, and what's the error as $\theta$ grows larger (which determines when we go from sufficiently small to an inaccurate model).

A final thought: I saw the Lorikeet Dreamweaver announcement where a business can set a goal, and for each customer, the AI can proactively do things to help the business achieve the goal. This is very similar to the Instinct, Muse and Dots product group, but now targeted for businesses. Instead of businesses, what if we directed our attention to how we might make ourselves flourish? Like, if an AI assistant can make proactive suggestions to maximise our opportunity space. A lot of us know what it would take to be truly awesome at something. However, it's difficult to do that and much easier to do the lazy, easy dopamine things (though, [*L'appetit vient en mangeant*](https://x.com/kepano/status/1682397456443781126)). It might be harder because we have to conjure everything by ourselves, but if you had a lil' muse guy wanting to see you be the best you you can be, it might just be the catalyst to want that for yourself too.

4 problems. A truly cooked problem today disguised so simply. The problem is a hexagon with two side lengths 7 and four side lengths 20 is inscribed in a circle. Find the radius. The first part of this is finding out what such a hexagon _could_ look like. There's three cases here, the two 7 side length are adjacent, one away from each other, or opposite. Each of these can be transformed to the other cases (and this is the key thing here) _without_ the circle changing. Put another way, the hexagon transformations preserve the circle. This means that no matter which hexagon, the circumscribed circle's radius will be the same for all of them.

![Two reflections connect all three hexagon arrangements while preserving the circle and its radius](/diagrams/5cff29633387305418a598cfecea6d77c2d0723488ebfd6a1cb91c2289e475cc.svg)

We choose the hexagon where the shorter side lengths are opposite each other, and look at the isosceles trapezium to find the radius.

Long time coming, but I finally bit the bullet and [re-learnt factorising quadratics where the leading coefficient isn't 1](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/algebra/x2f8bb11595b61c86:quadratics-multiplying-factoring/x2f8bb11595b61c86:factor-quadratics-grouping/a/factoring-quadratics-leading-coefficient-not-1), and there's no factor in any of the other terms. It's simple stuff, but it was biting me when I get to factorising and lose my flow to wolfram alpha.

5 problems (357-361) in ~1hr10. Touched on centroid bisects medians in a 2:1 ratio, and using that in a similarity problem within an inscribed circle. The difficulty for that problem tbh is drawing the right picture. For example, drawing the equilateral triangles on top of each other will directly get us getting the ratio of their altitudes.



No particularly hard problems this session. We intuitively know that for parallel tangents on the same circle, their points of tangency are collinear with the center of the circle. However, I couldn't find an intuitive direct proof for this, and had to use contradiction (suppose that they weren't collinear, then the co-interior angles of the parallel lines couldn't be supplementary).

Meta learning: immediately writing down the next problem as a rote activity helps to keep me focused and lessens the chance I doom-scroll on twitter between questions.

Chapter 5 on standard deviations. This one about abuse of graphs and figures to tell misleading stories about data. The one that most stuck out to me is a mistake I've made in the past: always prioritise conveying the data and story well, over making your graph being visually compelling. During the my IMC internship final presentation, I was so focused on making the components in a system diagram "look cool". Normally, these components would be boxes, connected to other components they interact with via lines. In my case, I added all these fancy line joinery, made the boxes look like chips, and while I enjoyed it, I definitely could've used that time to instead prepare better insights to communicate about my project. 

The rest of the chapter has more on inspecting the axis, how omitting zero can allow for arbitrary magnitude comparisons between different lines on the graph, and a couple of other things, but that's all known stuff. USUALLY, when these are forgotten, someone's trying to forward an agenda with a misconstrued graph.

Day 4 ✅ Learnt about [ujjayi breathing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IQrsJ-yZWV8) because I was like, how the hell is she inhaling and making such a loud noise. Most of my inhales through the nose are silent! Turns out it's a breathing technique, where you slightly restrict the back of the throat (almost like you're a quarter way through a snore?) and you get that audible sound, followed by an aggressive, try to fog up the mirror without opening your mouth exhale. No idea if it's useful, but a cool internal movement technique that you can sync up with external moves e.g. each move is preceded by an inhale / exhale, and you do moves at your breathing pace.

Finished cooking some shawarma using the [miya miya recipe](https://www.joshuaweissman.com/recipes/the-best-homemade-chicken-shawarma-sandwich-recipe). Way too much clove (the 4g of cloves in the recipe must be wrong), and I also should've cooked it across two sheet trays instead of basically boiling it in one. Made toum as well, first trying a [handstick blender technique](https://forksandfoliage.com/easiest-toum-garlic-dip/), but that didn't emulsify the oil correctly, so had to whip out the egg white to save the broken mixture. Using egg whites makes it feel more like a smooth mayonaise-y emulsion which isn't what I want from a THICK toum. Next time, let's not be lazy and just get the food processor out to do the job right, especially for a larger batch size that'll be in the fridge for a bit.

The fattoush came out amazing though. Used fried tortilla wraps as the crispy bits on top, and chucked cucumbers, shallots, tomatoes, mint, parsley and different lettuces all together with a sumac, pomegranate molasses vinaigrette.

Math: Working through AOPS geometry, final pset chapter. Pulleys and a memory hook for the angle-bisector theorem.

For the taut band around pulleys of radii 4 ft and 1 ft, with centres 6 ft apart, I split the length into two straight common tangents and two circular arcs. The useful construction is a rectangle that leaves a right triangle and short leg equal to the difference of the radii (due to the rectangle "short side" being the radii of the smaller circle)

$$
\ell=\sqrt{6^2-(4-1)^2}=3\sqrt3.
$$

The contact arcs are $240^\circ$ and $120^\circ$, giving

$$
L=2(3\sqrt3)+\frac{240}{360}(8\pi)+\frac{120}{360}(2\pi)
=6(\sqrt3+\pi)\text{ ft}.
$$

If both radii grow by $\epsilon$, their difference stays fixed, so the right triangle, straight lengths and contact angles stay unchanged. The two arcs together gain

$$
\Delta L=\left(\frac{240}{360}+\frac{120}{360}\right)2\pi\epsilon
=2\pi\epsilon,\qquad 0<\epsilon<\tfrac12\text{ ft}.
$$


For the angle-bisector theorem, if $BD$ bisects $\angle ABC$ and meets $AC$ at $D$,

$$
\frac{[ABD]}{[CBD]}=\frac{AD}{DC}=\frac{AB}{BC}.
$$

Bases $AD,DC$ share a height from $B$; bases $AB,BC$ have equal perpendicular heights from $D$. It's kinda like computing the area of the two triangles two different ways.
